theoryAdd.text: Going Deeper: Conduction Angle, Output Stages and Power

The conduction angle follows directly from the bias. If a transistor starts to conduct only when the input sine wave V_p sin ωt exceeds some threshold V_on (its V_BE of about 0.7 V, plus any reverse bias V_BB applied to the base), it conducts between the angles where V_p sin ωt = V_on. That interval is 180° − 2 arcsin(V_on/V_p), which is the same as 2 arccos(V_on/V_p). With V_on = 0 the angle is exactly 180° (ideal class B); with a reverse bias it is less than 180° (class C); and with a forward pre-bias the threshold becomes negative and the angle exceeds 180° (class AB).

theoryAdd.plainText: θc = 2 arccos(V_on / V_p), V_on = input level at which conduction starts

theoryAdd.text: The simplest output stage is a class A emitter follower biased by a constant current source I from the negative rail. Its output can rise to nearly +V_CC, but it can fall only to −I R_L, because at that point the whole bias current flows in the load and the transistor cuts off. Choosing I = V_CC/R_L gives a symmetrical swing of ±V_CC, and the efficiency is then η = (1/4)(V_m/IR_L)(V_m/V_CC), which peaks at 25 %. With no signal the follower still dissipates V_CC × I, so it runs hottest at idle.

In a complementary class B stage with supplies ±V_CC, each supply delivers half-sine current pulses of peak I_m = V_m/R_L, whose average is I_m/π. The total supply power is therefore 2V_CC V_m/(π R_L), while the load receives V_m²/(2R_L). Whatever is left is heat shared equally by the two transistors, and it is greatest not at full output but at V_m = 2V_CC/π.

theoryAdd.latex: P_L = \frac{V_m^2}{2R_L}, \quad P_S = \frac{2V_{CC}V_m}{\pi R_L}, \quad P_D = P_S - P_L
theoryAdd.plainText: PL = Vm²/(2RL); PS = 2 VCC Vm/(π RL); PD = PS − PL (class B, ±VCC)

theoryAdd.text:
Worked example 1: complementary class B, VCC = +/-18 V, RL = 8 ohm, Vm = 15 V
Im = 15/8 = 1.875 A
PL = 15^2/(2 x 8) = 14.06 W
PS = 2 x 18 x 1.875/pi = 21.49 W
eta = 14.06/21.49 = 65.4 %   (check: (pi/4)(15/18) = 65.4 %)
PD (both) = 21.49 - 14.06 = 7.42 W, i.e. 3.71 W per transistor
Worst case per transistor = 18^2/(pi^2 x 8) = 4.10 W at Vm = 2 x 18/pi = 11.46 V

Worked example 2: class A emitter follower, VCC = +/-12 V, RL = 60 ohm, I = 0.2 A
Negative swing limit = -I RL = -12 V, so a 10 V peak output is undistorted
PL = 10^2/(2 x 60) = 0.833 W
PS = 2 VCC I = 2 x 12 x 0.2 = 4.8 W (constant, signal or not)
eta = 0.833/4.8 = 17.4 %   (check: (1/4)(10/12)(10/12) = 17.4 %)
Idle dissipation of the follower = VCC x I = 12 x 0.2 = 2.4 W

Crossover distortion is easy to quantify. In an unbiased complementary pair the output stays at zero while |v_in| is below V_BE(on), so the output peak is V_p − 0.7 V and each transistor conducts for 2 arccos(0.7/V_p). With a 1.4 V peak input that is only 120° per device, leaving a dead zone of 60° around every zero crossing. For class D the losses are of a different kind: a MOSFET with on-resistance R_on in series with the load wastes I²R_on while on, so conduction efficiency is R_L/(R_L + R_on), and every transition adds a switching loss that grows with the switching frequency.

Common slips: using V_m²/R_L instead of V_m²/(2R_L) for load power (peak versus rms); treating the class B supply current as I_m instead of 2I_m/π; assuming class B dissipation is greatest at full output; and forgetting that a class A stage dissipates most with no signal at all.

Two numbers to remember: class B efficiency is proportional to V_m (halve the swing, halve η), while class A efficiency is proportional to V_m² (halve the swing, quarter η). Each class B transistor must be rated for about 0.2 × the maximum output power.

questions.questionText: The conduction angle of each output transistor in a class AB stage is:
questions.explanation: Class AB is biased slightly above cut-off, so each device conducts for a little more than half a cycle but less than the full cycle.

questions.questionText: An amplifier whose transistor conducts for only 120° of each input cycle is operating in:
questions.explanation: A conduction angle below 180° defines class C; class B is exactly 180°, class AB between 180° and 360°, and class A the full 360°.

questions.questionText: A transistor in a power stage conducts for 270° of each input cycle. Its class of operation is:
questions.explanation: 270° lies between 180° and 360°, which is class AB.

questions.questionText: In a class C amplifier the base of an npn transistor is biased:
options: At the centre of the DC load line
Below cut-off, with a reverse (negative) DC bias, so only the input peaks cause conduction
Exactly at cut-off with zero base bias
Slightly above cut-off with a small forward bias
questions.explanation: Class C places the Q-point beyond cut-off, so the input must first overcome the reverse bias and V_BE before any collector current flows, giving conduction for less than 180°.

questions.questionText: The low-pass LC filter at the output of a class D amplifier is needed to:
options: Remove the high-frequency switching component and leave the amplified audio signal
Generate the triangle carrier for the modulator
Bias the MOSFETs at the edge of conduction
Store energy between current pulses at the signal frequency, as in a class C tank
questions.explanation: The switches produce a full-amplitude PWM square wave; the filter passes its slowly varying average (the audio) and rejects the switching frequency and its harmonics.

questions.questionText: Crossover distortion in an unbiased complementary class B stage is caused by:
options: Both transistors conducting simultaneously near the zero crossing
Saturation of the transistors at the signal peaks
Neither transistor conducting while the input is below about ±0.7 V
The output coupling capacitor blocking low frequencies
questions.explanation: Each base-emitter junction needs about 0.7 V to turn on, so for small input levels around zero both transistors are off and the output stays at zero, producing a step at each crossing.

questions.questionText: An unbiased complementary class B emitter-follower stage uses silicon transistors (V_BE(on) = 0.7 V). The input is a sine wave of 5 V peak. Ignoring other losses, the peak output voltage is:
questions.explanation: The output follows the input minus one V_BE drop: 5 − 0.7 = 4.3 V. Subtracting 2V_BE (3.6 V) confuses it with the voltage between the two bases.

questions.questionText: An unbiased complementary class B stage has V_BE(on) = 0.7 V for each transistor and is driven by a 1.4 V peak sine wave. For how many degrees of each cycle does each transistor conduct?
questions.explanation: Conduction starts when 1.4 sin θ = 0.7, i.e. θ = 30°, and ends at 150°, so each device conducts for 150° − 30° = 120° instead of the ideal 180°.

questions.questionText: An emitter follower is widely used as a power output stage mainly because it:
options: Conducts for less than 180° and is therefore very efficient
Inverts the signal, cancelling even harmonics
Has a low output resistance and so can drive a low-resistance load without losing gain
questions.explanation: The follower's output resistance is only about r_e plus the source resistance divided by β, so a loudspeaker of a few ohms receives almost the full voltage; its voltage gain is just below 1.

questions.questionText: A class A emitter-follower output stage runs from ±12 V, drives R_L = 100 Ω and is biased by a 120 mA constant current source. Ignoring saturation voltages, its efficiency at the largest undistorted output is:
A series-fed class A amplifier with V_CC = 20 V and a collector load of 20 Ω is biased at the centre of its load line. The maximum AC power it can deliver to the load is:
questions.explanation: Peak voltage = V_CC/2 = 10 V and peak current = I_CQ = 0.5 A, so P_ac = (10 × 0.5)/2 = 2.5 W, i.e. V_CC²/(8R_L). The 10 W figure is the DC input power.

questions.questionText: A series-fed class A stage with V_CC = 24 V and R_C = 24 Ω is biased at I_CQ = 0.5 A. A signal produces a sinusoidal collector current of 0.3 A peak. Its efficiency is:
questions.explanation: P_ac = I_p² R_C/2 = 0.09 × 24/2 = 1.08 W; P_dc = V_CC I_CQ = 12 W; η = 1.08/12 = 9 %. Forgetting the 1/2 of the rms conversion gives 18 %.

questions.questionText: A transformer-coupled class A amplifier operates from V_CC = 12 V with a quiescent collector current of 250 mA. The maximum AC power it can deliver to the load (ideal transformer) is:
questions.explanation: P_dc = 12 × 0.25 = 3 W, and the theoretical maximum efficiency of transformer-coupled class A is 50 %, so P_ac(max) = 1.5 W. The 0.75 W figure uses the 25 % series-fed limit.

questions.questionText: In a transformer-coupled class A amplifier with V_CC = 10 V, the collector voltage swings between 4 V and 16 V. Using η = 50 % × [(V_max − V_min)/(V_max + V_min)]², its efficiency is:
A class B push-pull stage with V_CC = 20 V delivers a sine output of 10 V peak. Its efficiency is approximately:
questions.explanation: η = (π/4)(V_m/V_CC) = 0.785 × 10/20 = 39.3 %. The 78.5 % limit applies only at full swing V_m = V_CC.

questions.questionText: A complementary class B stage runs from ±15 V and drives an 8 Ω load with an output of 12 V peak. The total DC power drawn from the two supplies is approximately:
questions.explanation: I_m = 12/8 = 1.5 A; each supply provides an average of I_m/π, so P_S = 2V_CC I_m/π = 2 × 15 × 1.5/π = 14.3 W. The 9 W figure is the load power.

questions.questionText: A complementary class B stage with supplies of ±20 V drives an 8 Ω load with 16 V peak output. The power dissipated in each output transistor is approximately:
questions.explanation: I_m = 2 A; P_S = 2 × 20 × 2/π = 25.46 W; P_L = 16²/(2 × 8) = 16 W; P_D = 9.46 W for the pair, so 4.73 W per transistor.

questions.questionText: A complementary class B amplifier uses ±12 V supplies and an 8 Ω load. The maximum power that each transistor may have to dissipate, over all signal levels, is approximately:
questions.explanation: Worst-case dissipation occurs at V_m = 2V_CC/π and totals 2V_CC²/(π²R_L) = 2 × 144/(9.87 × 8) = 3.65 W, which is 1.82 W per transistor.

questions.questionText: Ignoring saturation voltages, the maximum sine-wave power a complementary class B stage with ±15 V supplies can deliver into an 8 Ω load is:
questions.explanation: At full swing V_m = V_CC = 15 V: P_L = V_m²/(2R_L) = 225/16 = 14.1 W. Using V_m²/R_L gives 28.1 W.

questions.questionText: A class B complementary stage is designed for a maximum sine output of 20 W. The worst-case dissipation for which each output transistor must be rated is approximately:
questions.explanation: Per-transistor worst case V_CC²/(π²R_L) divided by P_L(max) = V_CC²/(2R_L) is 2/π² = 0.203, so each device needs about 0.203 × 20 = 4.05 W; 8.1 W is for the pair.

questions.questionText: In a class B push-pull stage with V_CC = 18 V, the transistor dissipation is greatest when the peak output voltage is approximately:
questions.explanation: Dissipation peaks at V_m = 2V_CC/π = 36/π = 11.5 V, not at full output.

questions.questionText: A series-fed class A stage has V_CC = 12 V, R_C = 6 Ω and a quiescent current of 1 A. With no input signal, the power dissipated in the transistor is:
questions.explanation: V_CEQ = 12 − 1 × 6 = 6 V, so P_D = V_CEQ × I_CQ = 6 W. The supply delivers 12 W, of which the other 6 W heats R_C.

questions.questionText: In a class A power amplifier, the power dissipated in the transistor is greatest when:
options: The output is at its maximum undistorted swing
The output swing is 63.7 % of V_CC
The load is open-circuited during full swing
questions.explanation: The DC input power of class A is constant; P_D = P_dc − P_ac, so the transistor dissipates most when P_ac = 0, i.e. at idle.

questions.questionText: Which statement about power dissipation in a class B push-pull stage is correct?
options: It is greatest with no signal, as in class A
It rises continuously and is greatest at full output swing
It is independent of the signal level
It is zero with no signal and reaches its maximum at a peak output of about 0.64 V_CC
questions.explanation: With zero quiescent current there is no idle loss; P_D = P_S − P_L rises and then falls with swing, peaking at V_m = 2V_CC/π ≈ 0.637 V_CC.

questions.questionText: A class AB complementary output stage runs from ±15 V and is biased at a quiescent current of 20 mA. The power drawn from the supplies with no signal is:
questions.explanation: The quiescent current flows from +15 V through both transistors to −15 V, a total of 30 V: P = 30 × 0.02 = 0.6 W. Zero would be true only for pure class B.

questions.questionText: The output of an unbiased class B stage driven by a small sine wave shows a flat step each time the waveform passes through zero. This defect is called:
questions.explanation: The flat step around the zero crossing, where neither transistor conducts, is crossover distortion; clipping occurs at the peaks.

questions.questionText: A class C amplifier is driven at 10 MHz and its collector tank is tuned to 30 MHz. The output frequency is:
questions.explanation: The pulsed collector current is rich in harmonics; a tank tuned to the third harmonic selects 3 × 10 = 30 MHz, so the stage acts as a frequency tripler.

questions.questionText: In a class C stage the transistor begins to conduct only when the input exceeds 2.0 V (reverse bias plus V_BE). If the input is a sine wave of 2.83 V peak, the conduction angle is approximately:
questions.explanation: Conduction begins where 2.83 sin θ = 2.0, i.e. θ ≈ 45°, and ends at 135°, so θ_c = 135° − 45° = 90° (equivalently 2 arccos(2.0/2.83)).

questions.questionText: A class C stage cannot be used as a wide-band audio amplifier because:
options: Its efficiency is too low for audio power levels
It requires a complementary npn-pnp pair
Its collector current is a train of narrow pulses, and a sine output is restored only by a load tuned to one frequency
questions.explanation: Without a tuned tank the output would be the distorted pulse train itself; the tank works at a single frequency, which is unsuitable for a broadband audio signal.

questions.questionText: A class D half-bridge switches its output between 0 V and 24 V. When the duty cycle is 0.6, the average (filtered) output voltage is:
questions.explanation: V_o(avg) = D × V_DD = 0.6 × 24 = 14.4 V; 9.6 V would be the result of using the off-time fraction.

questions.questionText: In a class D stage only one MOSFET conducts at a time, each having an on-resistance of 0.1 Ω, and the load is 8 Ω. Neglecting switching and filter losses, the efficiency is approximately:
questions.explanation: The on-switch is in series with the load, so η = R_L/(R_L + R_on) = 8/8.1 = 98.8 %. 1.2 % is the fraction lost, not the efficiency.

questions.questionText: In a class D amplifier the pulse-width-modulated drive signal is usually generated by:
options: Passing the input through a tuned LC tank
Comparing the input signal with a high-frequency triangle wave in a comparator
Rectifying the input with a bridge rectifier
Biasing the output transistors slightly above cut-off
questions.explanation: The comparator output is high whenever the input exceeds the triangle, so the pulse width follows the instantaneous input level.

questions.questionText: The output transistors of a class D amplifier dissipate very little power because:
options: When on their voltage is almost zero and when off their current is almost zero, so the V × I product stays small
They conduct for exactly 180° of each cycle
Their quiescent current is set just above cut-off
The output filter absorbs the heat
questions.explanation: Dissipation is the product of device voltage and current; a switch that is fully on or fully off keeps one of them near zero except during the brief transitions.

questions.questionText: A class D audio amplifier must reproduce signals up to 20 kHz. Which switching frequency is the most suitable?
questions.explanation: The switching frequency must be many times the highest audio frequency so the output filter can remove it without affecting the audio band; 400 kHz is 20 times 20 kHz.

questions.questionText: In a complementary-symmetry class B output stage, during the positive half-cycle of the input:
options: The pnp transistor conducts and the npn transistor is cut off
The npn transistor conducts and the pnp transistor is cut off
questions.explanation: A positive input forward-biases the npn base-emitter junction and reverse-biases the pnp one, so the npn device sources current into the load; the roles reverse on the negative half-cycle.

questions.questionText: Which statement about a complementary-symmetry push-pull output stage is correct?
options: It requires both transistors to be of the same polarity (both npn)
It needs a phase-splitter to produce two antiphase drive signals
It needs no centre-tapped transformer, because the joined emitters of the npn and pnp devices drive the load directly
It cannot be operated from a single supply
questions.explanation: The opposite polarities of the npn and pnp devices mean one input signal turns on one device per half-cycle, so no phase splitter or transformer is needed; a single supply with an output capacitor also works.

questions.questionText: A complementary class B stage is powered from a single 24 V supply, with the midpoint coupled to an 8 Ω load through a large capacitor. Ignoring saturation voltages, the maximum sine output power is:
questions.explanation: The midpoint sits at 12 V, so the peak swing is V_CC/2 = 12 V and P = 12²/(2 × 8) = 9 W. Using the full 24 V gives 36 W.

questions.questionText: A complementary class B amplifier must deliver 25 W of sine power into an 8 Ω load. If each transistor has V_CE(sat) = 2 V, the minimum symmetrical supply voltage is:
questions.explanation: V_m = √(2 P R_L) = √(2 × 25 × 8) = 20 V peak; allowing 2 V saturation, V_CC = 20 + 2 = 22 V on each rail. 14.1 V is the rms output.

questions.questionText: In a transformer-coupled class B push-pull amplifier each transistor carries half-sine pulses of 3 A peak. The average current drawn from the single supply is approximately:
questions.explanation: Each transistor averages I_m/π = 0.955 A and both draw from the same supply, so I_dc = 2I_m/π = 1.91 A. 2.12 A is the rms value of a 3 A sine.

questions.questionText: In a class B push-pull stage, reducing the peak output voltage to half its previous value changes the efficiency to:
options: One quarter of its previous value
questions.explanation: η = (π/4)(V_m/V_CC) is directly proportional to V_m, so halving the swing halves the efficiency. In class A, where η is proportional to V_m², it would fall to one quarter.

questions.questionText: A series-fed class A amplifier with V_CC = 24 V is biased at the centre of its load line. When the peak output voltage is 6 V, its efficiency is:
questions.explanation: At centre bias P_dc = V_CC²/(2R_C) and P_ac = V_m²/(2R_C), so η = (V_m/V_CC)² = (6/24)² = 6.25 %. Class A efficiency falls with the square of the swing.

questions.questionText: A series-fed (resistive-load) class A stage is limited to 25 % efficiency, whereas a transformer-coupled one can reach 50 %, because:
options: The transformer-coupled stage conducts for only 180°
The transformer adds energy to the signal
The series-fed stage has a higher quiescent current for the same load
In the series-fed stage the DC collector current also flows in the load resistor, wasting power and limiting the swing to V_CC/2
questions.explanation: With a transformer the load carries no DC and the collector can swing from nearly 0 to 2V_CC, doubling the AC output for the same DC input power.

questions.questionText: The theoretical maximum efficiency π/4 of a class B push-pull stage is reached when:
options: The peak output voltage equals the supply voltage V_CC
The quiescent current is set at a few milliamperes
questions.explanation: η = (π/4)(V_m/V_CC) reaches its maximum of 78.5 % only when V_m = V_CC; at 2V_CC/π the transistor dissipation is maximum instead.

questions.questionText: Which statement about output-stage classes is NOT correct?
options: A class A transistor conducts for the whole cycle
Each class B transistor conducts for half of each cycle
A class C transistor conducts for more than 180° of each cycle
Class D output transistors operate as switches
questions.explanation: Class C conducts for less than 180°, which is why it needs a tuned load; the other three statements are the standard definitions.

questions.questionText: A class A emitter-follower output stage uses ±15 V supplies, a 0.2 A constant current source as its emitter bias, and a 50 Ω load. Ignoring saturation voltages, the largest symmetrical (undistorted) peak output voltage is:
questions.explanation: The output can rise to about +15 V but can fall only to −I R_L = −0.2 × 50 = −10 V before the transistor cuts off, so the symmetrical limit is 10 V peak.

questions.questionText: A class A emitter-follower output stage with ±15 V supplies, 0.2 A constant-current emitter bias and a 50 Ω load delivers a 10 V peak sine output. Its efficiency is approximately:
questions.explanation: P_L = 10²/(2 × 50) = 1 W; the supplies deliver 2 × 15 × 0.2 = 6 W regardless of signal; η = 1/6 = 16.7 %. Counting only one supply gives 33.3 %.
